title: Germline Change: Reproductive and Genetic Engineering Technologies
subtitle: Changing which alleles are passed on, versus changing the DNA that is passed on
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: investigate the uses and advantages of current genetic technologies that induce genetic change
distinguish between somatic mutations and germ-line mutations and their effect on an organism (ACSBL082, ACSBL083)
Compare germline genetic changes in reproductive and genetic engineering biotechnologies
Use examples to compare transgenic organisms and genetically modified organisms
inquiryQuestion: Does artificial manipulation of DNA have the potential to change populations forever?
lessonIntent: Students can compare germline genetic change caused by reproductive technologies (which change allele combinations and frequencies) with genetic engineering (which changes the inherited DNA sequence), and distinguish both from somatic change.
examSkill: Classify a technology as reproductive or genetic engineering, state whether it changes the germline, and explain how the change reaches the next generation.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome back to HSC Biology. Today, germline change in reproductive and genetic engineering technologies. Let's get into it.

scenes.caption: Germline Change: Reproductive and Genetic Engineering Technologies (Year 12 Biology, Module 6, Lesson 13)

scenes.heading: Two ways to change the next generation
scenes.body: Artificial insemination lets one bull father thousands of calves. Bt cotton passes a bacterial gene to every seed. Only one of these changes a DNA sequence.
scenes.callout: Both change what the next generation inherits, but in completely different ways.
scenes.caption: Artificial insemination and Bt cotton both change the germline, but only one changes a DNA sequence.

voiceover.text: Here are two ways people are changing what gets passed to the next generation. On a dairy farm, artificial insemination lets one top bull father thousands of calves, so his alleles spread through the herd in a single generation. And in a cotton field, most of Australia's crop is genetically modified to carry genes from a soil bacterium, Bacillus thuringiensis, which make a protein that's toxic to caterpillar pests, and the seeds inherit those genes. Both of these change the germline, the genetic material passed on through reproduction. But they change it in completely different ways. One changes which alleles get passed on, and the other changes the DNA sequence itself. Today we'll compare them properly, and learn to say exactly what kind of change each technology makes.

scenes.heading: Germline change versus somatic change
scenes.body: Whether a change is inherited depends on which cells carry it.

bullets.text: Germline change: in gametes, or the cells or embryo that make them, so it is inherited.
Somatic change: in body cells only, so it affects one individual and is not inherited.
Only germline change can alter a population over generations.

scenes.callout: Ask: will the next generation inherit it?
scenes.caption: Germline changes are inherited; somatic changes affect only the individual.
scenes.recapSeed: Germline change is inherited; somatic change is not.

voiceover.text: First, the key distinction for this whole lesson. A germline change is found in the gametes, the eggs or sperm, or in the cells or early embryo that will go on to make them. That means it gets inherited by offspring. A somatic change, on the other hand, is only in body cells, like skin, blood or muscle, so it affects that one individual and dies with them. That's why a gene therapy that fixes a patient's blood cells isn't passed to their children. And here's why it matters. Only germline change can alter a population over generations, which is exactly what reproductive and genetic engineering technologies set out to do. So for any technology, the first question is simple, will the next generation inherit this change.

scenes.heading: The words you need

bullets.text: Germline: the gametes and the cells that give rise to them, the DNA passed to offspring.
Reproductive technology: a tool that controls how gametes or embryos are brought together.
Recombinant DNA: DNA formed by combining genetic material from different sources.
Transgenic organism: an organism carrying DNA from a different species.
Genetically modified organism: any organism whose DNA has been deliberately altered, transgenic or not.

scenes.callout: Every transgenic organism is a GMO, but not every GMO is transgenic.
scenes.caption: Germline, reproductive technology, recombinant DNA, transgenic organism, GMO.

voiceover.text: Five terms to map the field. The germline is the gametes and the cells that give rise to them, so it's the DNA that actually gets passed to offspring. A reproductive technology controls how gametes or embryos are brought together, like artificial insemination, artificial pollination, or IVF and embryo transfer. Recombinant DNA is DNA formed by combining genetic material from different sources. A transgenic organism carries DNA from a different species, like Bt cotton with its bacterial genes. And a genetically modified organism, or GMO, is any organism whose DNA has been deliberately altered. That last pair is worth getting right. Every transgenic organism is a GMO, but a GMO made by editing its own genes, with nothing added from another species, is not transgenic.

scenes.heading: Two ways to change the germline
scenes.body: Reproductive technologies change which alleles are passed on. Genetic engineering changes the sequence that is passed on.

bullets.text: Reproductive technologies choose the parents, so allele combinations and frequencies change.
Genetic engineering alters the DNA in a cell that becomes the whole organism, including its gametes.
Reproductive control changes the combination; genetic engineering changes the sequence.

scenes.secondary: A transgene inserted into a single cell that then grows into a plant ends up in every cell, including the pollen and eggs, so it is inherited like any other gene.
scenes.callout: Combination versus sequence is the dividing line.
scenes.caption: Reproductive technologies change allele combinations; genetic engineering changes the inherited sequence.

voiceover.text: So how does each family change the germline. Reproductive technologies choose the parents. Artificial insemination, artificial pollination, and IVF with embryo transfer all decide which gametes combine, and how many offspring a chosen parent leaves. No sequence changes, but the combination of alleles in each offspring changes, and across a herd or a crop the allele frequencies shift, sometimes very quickly. Whole organism cloning is the extreme case, copying one genotype exactly, with no new combination at all. Genetic engineering works differently. The DNA is altered in a single cell, which then grows into the whole organism, so the new sequence ends up in every cell, including the pollen, eggs or sperm. From then on it's inherited like any other gene. The clean way to hold it is this, reproductive control changes the combination, and genetic engineering changes the sequence.

rows: One bull sires thousands of calves
Copies one genotype, no new combination
New sequence in every cell, inherited

scenes.heading: Comparing the outcomes
scenes.body: Both families change what the next generation inherits, but their advantages and risks differ.

bullets.text: Reproductive: fast spread of desirable alleles, but no new alleles and a narrower gene pool.
Genetic engineering: adds traits the species never had, but a transgene can spread by gene flow.
Human germline editing is illegal in Australia, because the change would be inherited.

scenes.secondary: GMOs in Australia are regulated by the Office of the Gene Technology Regulator. In 2018, He Jiankui's gene-edited twins showed why heritable human editing is so tightly restricted.
scenes.callout: Same target, the next generation; different risks.
scenes.caption: Reproductive technologies spread existing alleles; genetic engineering adds new ones; both change inheritance.

voiceover.text: Now compare the outcomes, because both families have real advantages and real risks. Reproductive technologies spread desirable alleles fast, one elite bull can improve a whole herd in a generation. But they add no new alleles, and relying on a few top parents narrows the gene pool, which can bring hidden recessive disorders together. Genetic engineering can add a trait the species never had, like pest resistance in Bt cotton, which has sharply cut insecticide spraying on Australian cotton. But once a transgene is in the germline, it could spread to related plants by gene flow, which is why GMOs here are regulated by the Office of the Gene Technology Regulator. And for humans the line is firm. Making a heritable change to the human genome is illegal in Australia, and the gene edited twins announced by He Jiankui in twenty eighteen show exactly why.

scenes.heading: Is the germline changed, and how?
scenes.question: For each case, state whether the germline is changed, and if so whether it is the allele combination or the DNA sequence: (a) one champion bull is used to inseminate a whole herd; (b) a Bt gene is inserted into a cotton cell, which is grown into a plant; (c) a patient's blood stem cells are edited with CRISPR to treat sickle cell disease.
scenes.coachNote: Ask two questions: is it inherited, and does the sequence change or just the combination?
steps: (a) Germline changed through reproduction: the calves inherit the bull's alleles, so allele combinations and herd frequencies change, but no sequence is altered.
(b) Germline changed through genetic engineering: the transgene is in every cell of the plant, including pollen and eggs, so the new sequence is inherited.
(c) Not a germline change: only somatic blood cells are edited, so the patient's children do not inherit it.
Decision rule: combination (reproductive), sequence (genetic engineering), or somatic (not inherited).
Answer: (a) germline, combination; (b) germline, sequence; (c) somatic, not inherited.
scenes.caption: (a) germline, combination; (b) germline, sequence; (c) somatic, not inherited.

voiceover.text: Let's classify three cases. Part a, one champion bull is used to inseminate a whole herd. The calves inherit his alleles, so the germline of the herd has changed, but only through reproduction. The allele combinations and frequencies shift, and no sequence is altered. Part b, a Bt gene is inserted into a single cotton cell, which is then grown into a whole plant. The transgene ends up in every cell, including the pollen and eggs, so this is a germline change through genetic engineering, a new sequence that gets inherited. Part c, a patient's blood stem cells are edited with CRISPR to treat sickle cell disease. That's a trap. Only somatic blood cells are changed, so the patient's children won't inherit it, which makes it not a germline change at all. So the decision rule is combination, sequence, or somatic.

scenes.heading: Three distinctions to keep clear
scenes.body: Trap 1: blurring reproductive control with DNA change. Choosing parents changes the combination, not the sequence.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: assuming all genetic engineering is inherited. Somatic gene therapy changes only the patient. Trap 3: thinking reproductive technologies cannot change a population. By shifting allele frequencies and narrowing the gene pool, they can change it quickly.
scenes.callout: Combination versus sequence; germline versus somatic; reproduction can still reshape a population.
scenes.caption: Reproductive control is not DNA change; not all engineering is heritable; allele frequencies still shift.

voiceover.text: Three distinctions that separate a clear answer from a muddled one. Trap one, blurring reproductive control with DNA change. Choosing which parents breed changes the combination of alleles, but the sequence is untouched. Trap two, assuming that anything involving genetic engineering must be inherited. Somatic gene therapy edits a patient's body cells only, so it stops with that patient. Whether a change is heritable depends on which cells carry it, not on how clever the technique is. Trap three, thinking that because reproductive technologies don't alter DNA, they can't change a population. They absolutely can. Using a few elite parents shifts allele frequencies fast and narrows the gene pool, which is a genuine germline change at the population level. Combination versus sequence, germline versus somatic, keep those straight.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: A breeder uses embryo transfer to spread an elite cow's genes through a herd, while a lab inserts a jellyfish gene into a plant. A student says both are genetic engineering because both change what offspring inherit. Where is the error?
answerSteps: Both do change what the next generation inherits, so both affect the germline.
Embryo transfer is a reproductive technology: it controls which parents breed, but no DNA sequence changes.
Inserting a jellyfish gene is recombinant DNA: it creates a transgenic organism with a new, inherited sequence.
The error is treating any germline change as genetic engineering.
Answer: embryo transfer changes the combination; only the gene insertion changes the sequence.
scenes.caption: Embryo transfer is reproductive control; only the gene insertion engineers DNA.

voiceover.text: Quick check. A breeder uses embryo transfer to spread an elite cow's genes through a herd, while in a lab someone inserts a jellyfish gene into a plant. A student says both are genetic engineering, because both change what the offspring inherit. Where's the error? Pause and reason it through. Right, the student is half right. Both do change what the next generation inherits, so both affect the germline. But embryo transfer is a reproductive technology. It controls which parents breed and how many offspring an elite animal leaves, and no DNA sequence changes. Inserting a jellyfish gene is recombinant DNA, which makes a transgenic organism with a new sequence that gets inherited. So the error is treating any germline change as genetic engineering. One changes the combination, the other changes the sequence.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Germline change is inherited; somatic change affects only one individual.
Reproductive technologies change allele combinations and frequencies, not sequences.
Genetic engineering changes the sequence, and the transgene is inherited.
Every transgenic organism is a GMO, but not every GMO is transgenic.
Heritable human genome editing is illegal in Australia.
scenes.finalPrompt: Classifying a technology? Ask: inherited or not, and combination or sequence?
scenes.caption: Five takeaways: germline vs somatic, combination vs sequence, transgenic vs GMO, human germline limits.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. Five things to take away. First, a germline change is inherited, while a somatic change affects only one individual. Second, reproductive technologies like artificial insemination, pollination and embryo transfer change allele combinations and frequencies, but not DNA sequences. Third, genetic engineering changes the sequence, and because the altered cell grows into the whole organism, the change is inherited. Fourth, every transgenic organism is a GMO, but not every GMO is transgenic. And fifth, making heritable changes to the human genome is illegal in Australia. Whenever you classify a technology, ask two things, is it inherited, and is it the combination or the sequence that changes. See you next lesson.
